prose_changes.old: It began in the winter of 1734-35 in Northampton, Massachusetts, where the town's minister, Jonathan Edwards, watched an ordinary Connecticut Valley congregation come apart and remake itself in a wave of conversions. And then did something unusual: he wrote down what had happened, case by case, including a young woman the town had thought beyond hope and a four-year-old girl. When the English preacher George Whitefield toured the colonies from 1739, scattered local revivals became a general one, with itinerants crossing parish lines and crowds gathering in the open air. It split New England's churches: the New Lights defended the awakening, the Old Lights — Charles Chauncy of Boston foremost among them — attacked it as enthusiasm and disorder, and hundreds of Separate congregations broke away, a great many of them becoming Baptist. It also produced the first substantial body of Christian writing by Black and Native people in the colonies.
prose_changes.new: It began in the winter of 1734-35 in Northampton, Massachusetts. There the town's minister, Jonathan Edwards, watched an ordinary church in the Connecticut Valley come apart and remake itself in a wave of conversions. Then he did something unusual: he wrote down what had happened, case by case. His cases included a young woman the town had thought beyond hope and a four-year-old girl. The English preacher George Whitefield toured the colonies from 1739, and scattered local revivals became a general one. Preachers crossed parish lines, and crowds met in the open air. The awakening split New England's churches. The New Lights defended it. The Old Lights, led by Charles Chauncy of Boston, attacked it as 'enthusiasm', false claims to the Spirit, and disorder. Hundreds of Separate congregations broke away. Many may later have become Baptist, though no text we hold yet traces them. Black and Native Christians of its world also began to write. prose_changes.old: On St Bartholomew's Day 1662 about two thousand ministers who could not accept the restored Prayer Book and episcopal ordination were put out of the Church of England, and English Presbyterianism and Congregationalism became permanently separate traditions rather than parties inside one church. Barred from the universities, they built their own: the dissenting academies, which taught mathematics, science and modern languages when Oxford and Cambridge largely did not, and educated a striking share of the country's scientists, manufacturers and reformers.
